passage: Asif had spent three weeks at the new hostel without telling anyone where he came from. When Karthik, the boy in the next room, asked about home, Asif almost gave his usual short answer. But the light in the corridor was warm and Karthik was peeling an orange, not scrolling his phone. So Asif said, "My grandmother's kitchen in Hyderabad, the smell of saffron rice on Eid mornings. Honestly, that's what I miss." Karthik nodded and shared a piece of orange. "Mine is my uncle's bike and dosa on Sunday." They talked till the lights went out. Asif did not mention the harder stories about his father, and he felt no need to. He would decide about that later, if he wanted.

qa.q: What did Karthik share with Asif while they talked?
qa.a: Karthik shared a piece of orange.

qa.q: Why did Asif decide to say more than usual about home, and what did he choose not to share?
qa.a: Asif felt comfortable because the corridor was warm and Karthik gave him full attention, and he chose not to mention his father because he felt no need to.

qa.q: What could Asif do if he later wanted to share more?
qa.a: He could wait until he feels safe and see whether Karthik shares back, then tell as much as he likes.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when Asif told him about the saffron rice?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt trusted and welcomed, which fits how he answered with his own memory of his uncle's bike and dosa.

grounding: Asif shares a family memory to be known while keeping harder details private by choice.

"You never said where your family's from," Indu said, stirring the pot of noodles in the dorm kitchen. Vaibhav shrugged. "Coastal Kerala, mostly. My grandfather fished. I don't tell people much, since they think it's boring."
"It's not boring. What was it like?"
"Loud at four in the morning. My mother still hums the boat songs." He hesitated. "Also, I'm the first one in the family at university."
"That's a big thing."
"Is it? It feels like a lot to explain."
"You don't have to explain more than you want. I'll tell you mine if you like. My family moved four times before I was ten."
Vaibhav laughed, relieved. "Okay. That one I definitely want to hear."

qa.q: What did Vaibhav's grandfather do?
qa.a: His grandfather fished.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav say he didn't tell people much, and what does his hesitation suggest?
qa.a: He says people think it's boring, and his hesitation suggests he is unsure it is safe to share, though he might simply be shy.

qa.q: What did Indu do that made it easier for Vaibhav to open up?
qa.a: She showed interest, told him he didn't have to explain more than he wanted, and offered a story of her own.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about Vaibhav trusting her with his memories?
qa.a: Indu probably feels glad and included, which is why she offered her own story back so the sharing stayed even.

grounding: Vaibhav shares family stories and background in his own time, with Indu respecting his choice.

passage: The first time I really told anyone about my family was in a college ice-breaker I was dreading. I'm Nilesh. We had to share one story from home. Ankita went first and talked about her grandmother's pickle shop in Nagpur, and everyone laughed. When it was my turn, I told them how my great-grandfather walked from Sindh to Mumbai in 1947 with only a copper pot, and how that pot sits on our shelf now. The room went quiet, then people asked questions. It felt good to be known a little. But when someone asked, "So what caste are you, then?", I felt my shoulders go tight. I said, "I'd rather not get into that." Ankita changed the subject for me without making a fuss. Later I told her about some harder parts of that migration story, the parts I hadn't shared with the whole room. That was my choice, and it felt right.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's great-grandfather's copper pot sit on now?
qa.a: On their shelf.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when asked about caste?
qa.a: Nilesh felt uncomfortable and guarded, shoulders going tight, and chose not to answer.

qa.q: What did Ankita do that helped?
qa.a: She changed the subject quietly without making a fuss, respecting Nilesh's choice not to share.

qa.q: How might the person who asked about caste have seen the question?
qa.a: They may have thought it was just curiosity, not realising it pushed for private details Nilesh didn't want to share.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing family history to be known while choosing what to keep private, and a friend respecting that.

passage:
Mentor's note, first-year orientation week, Thursday.
At our "Where I come from" evening, Pranav, a first-year, shared the story of his family's small tea stall in Siliguri and how his mother ran it alone after his father left. The group listened closely. Two students thanked him afterwards. Then one of the others asked, loudly, "And are you seeing anyone? You never talk about that." Pranav smiled tightly and said, "Some things I keep for later." The student pushed: "Come on, we're all sharing." I stepped in and said that everyone chooses what they share and when, and nobody owes the group private details. Pranav looked relieved. Afterwards I told him privately that he had handled it well and that my door is open anytime, for anything. I've also reminded the whole group in our chat that "sharing" nights are about choice.
— Pallavi

qa.q: Where was Pranav's family's tea stall?
qa.a: In Siliguri.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when the student pushed him to share?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and cornered, smiling tightly, and then relieved when Pallavi stepped in.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that protected Pranav's choice?
qa.a: She told the group that everyone chooses what to share and when, spoke to Pranav privately, and reminded the whole group that sharing is by choice.

qa.q: How might the student who pushed have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have thought sharing meant everyone should reveal everything, not realising it put pressure on Pranav.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing family history while keeping private details for later, and an adult protecting that choice.

passage:
Friday night.
Irawati and I finally went for that long walk by the lake. She told me about growing up in Pune, her grandfather's bookshop, how she learned Marathi and Kannada at the same time. So I told her about Eid at my Nani's house in Hyderabad, the thirty cousins, and the haleem my Ammi still makes every year. It felt so nice to be known like that.
Then she asked, "Do you wear a hijab at home?" I don't mind that question. But she followed with, "What do your parents think about you living alone?", and I noticed I didn't want to answer that one yet. There's a story there, and I don't know her well enough.
So I said, "That's a long one. Another time?" She just said, "Of course," and asked about the haleem recipe. I think we're going to be real friends.
— Hafsa

qa.q: Where did Hafsa's Nani live?
qa.a: In Hyderabad.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when Irawati asked about her parents' views?
qa.a: Hafsa felt hesitant and not yet ready to share, sensing it was a longer, private story.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that kept the conversation comfortable?
qa.a: Hafsa answered what felt easy, and gently postponed the harder question with "Another time?" instead of forcing an answer.

qa.q: How did Irawati respond to Hafsa's choice?
qa.a: She accepted it with "Of course" and moved on to the haleem recipe, which respected Hafsa's pace.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing cultural memories to be known while choosing which private details to keep for later.
